title: Leg 60 — Denver Ballparks, Red Rocks, and Longs
subtitle: Front Range cities, Coors Field, Red Rocks, the Flatirons and Longs Peak
preflightBriefing: Welcome aboard. We are leaving Cheyenne and following the Front Range south toward Denver before turning west for Red Rocks, then north past Boulder's Flatirons for a broad eastern view of Longs Peak and Rocky Mountain National Park. Coors Field will be a close visual target just west of our first waypoint. Red Rocks will be several miles off the left side of its viewing pass, the Flatirons will also be off the left, and Longs Peak will be much farther west, so I will be clear about where to look and how prominent each sight should be. I'll stay quiet while you taxi and depart. Once you're airborne and settled, say Trip continue.

blocks.title: South along the Front Range
blocks.text: We are leaving Cheyenne and heading south along the broad eastern edge of the Rockies. For most of this first stretch the mountains remain off to the right while the plains spread away to the left. The visual rhythm here is less about one landmark and more about the long Front Range corridor linking Wyoming with northern Colorado and Denver.

blocks.title: Wyoming into Colorado
blocks.text: As we cross from Wyoming into Colorado, the landscape barely acknowledges the political boundary. Ranch land, shortgrass prairie and the distant mountain wall continue almost unchanged. The big difference farther south is human scale: towns begin to string together more continuously along the Front Range.

blocks.title: Fort Collins off the right
blocks.text: Fort Collins is well off to the right of our route, roughly nine miles at our closest pass. Colorado State University there was established in 1870 as the state's land-grant institution. The school's original mission emphasized practical education in agriculture and the mechanical arts, fitting a region where farming, irrigation and livestock were central to settlement.

blocks.title: Greeley off the left
blocks.text: Greeley lies off to the left, also several miles from our track. It began in 1870 as the Union Colony, an experimental agricultural community organized by Nathan Meeker with backing from newspaper publisher Horace Greeley. Irrigation was fundamental from the beginning; colonists quickly dug ditches to turn the dry plains into productive farmland.

blocks.title: Water made the northern Front Range possible
blocks.text: Those early irrigation projects helped shape something much larger than individual farms. Competition over water between communities such as Greeley and Fort Collins pushed Colorado toward the legal system of prior appropriation, where older beneficial water uses generally receive priority over newer ones. In a dry state, water law became almost as important as land ownership.

blocks.title: The Front Range fills in
blocks.text: The farther south we go, the more the once-separated towns begin to merge into a continuous urban corridor. Interstate 25 follows the same north-south spine below, with the Rocky Mountains consistently defining the western horizon and the plains leaving room for expansion to the east.

blocks.title: A weapons plant turned wildlife refuge
blocks.text: As we near the Denver area, the Rocky Mountain Arsenal National Wildlife Refuge lies several miles off to the left. The site began as a World War Two chemical-weapons manufacturing complex, later handled Cold War production and demilitarization, and then underwent a massive cleanup. Today roughly fifteen thousand acres support wildlife including bison, bald eagles and black-footed ferrets.

blocks.title: Denver comes into view
blocks.text: Denver is now taking over the view ahead. The city grew from the 1858 gold-rush settlements along Cherry Creek and the South Platte, but its long-term importance came from becoming the commercial and transportation center for a much larger Rocky Mountain region.

blocks.title: Union Station and the railroad city
blocks.text: Near downtown, Union Station represents Denver's railroad era. The first Union Depot opened in 1881 with a tall central clock tower. After a fire and later rebuilding, the present main structure opened in 1914. By the mid-1940s, more than fifty thousand travelers a day could pass through during the station's busiest period.

blocks.title: Major League baseball arrives
blocks.text: Denver finally gained a Major League Baseball team in 1993. Before Coors Field was ready, the Rockies played at old Mile High Stadium. Their first home game drew 80,227 fans, and the expansion club quickly proved that the supposedly small Mountain Time Zone market had an enormous appetite for baseball.

blocks.title: Coors Field on the right
blocks.text: Coors Field should now be easy to pick out just to the right, less than a mile west of our flight path. Look for the large baseball stadium on the north side of downtown. This is a genuinely close pass, so unlike some of our more distant landmarks, you should have a reasonable chance of spotting it.

blocks.title: Coors Field at altitude
blocks.text: Coors Field opened for official Major League play in 1995. Its first game went fourteen innings before Dante Bichette ended it with a three-run home run. The altitude matters here: thinner air reduces drag on a baseball, and the Rockies note that a well-hit ball can travel noticeably farther in Denver than it would at sea level.

blocks.title: Across Denver toward the foothills
blocks.text: We are turning west now, leaving downtown and heading toward the first abrupt wall of the foothills. The city gives way quickly to older suburbs, hogbacks and red sandstone ridges that mark the transition from the plains into the Rockies.

blocks.title: Red Rocks off the left
blocks.text: Red Rocks is coming up off the left side. The amphitheatre itself is about four miles south of our viewing waypoint, so this is not an overhead pass. Look left toward the conspicuous red sandstone formations near the foothills rather than expecting the stage itself to fill the view.

blocks.title: The rocks before the music
blocks.text: The great red slabs around the amphitheatre belong to the Fountain Formation, sediments eroded from an ancient mountain range roughly three hundred million years ago. Later uplift tilted those layers steeply, creating the dramatic walls that eventually made this site such an unusual natural performance space.

blocks.title: Building the amphitheatre
blocks.text: The modern amphitheatre was built largely during the Depression with Civilian Conservation Corps labor. Workers spent years shaping the seating bowl between enormous natural rock walls, and the venue officially opened in 1941. Architect Burnham Hoyt deliberately tried to make the construction feel subordinate to the geology.

blocks.title: Beatles, U2 and one famous non-sellout
blocks.text: Red Rocks later became one of the world's most famous concert venues. The Beatles played here in 1964, and remarkably it was the only stop on their first American tour that did not sell out. Decades later, U2's 1983 concert film at Red Rocks helped turn the venue into an international music icon.

blocks.title: North along the foothills
blocks.text: We are turning north now with the foothills on the left and the Denver metropolitan area falling behind. This edge between plains and mountains is one of the most visually distinctive parts of Colorado because tilted sedimentary layers repeatedly form long ridges, hogbacks and fins.

blocks.title: Boulder ahead-left
blocks.text: Boulder is coming into the scene ahead and to the left. The city sits hard against the foothills, with open space deliberately preserved along much of its western edge. That gives the mountain backdrop an unusually sharp boundary against the city.

blocks.title: The Flatirons on the left
blocks.text: The Flatirons should now be prominent off the left side, about four miles west of our route. Look for the great tilted slabs leaning against Green Mountain. Their nickname comes from their resemblance to old-fashioned household flat irons.

blocks.title: A landmark in American climbing
blocks.text: The Flatirons are also deeply tied to Colorado climbing history. The City of Boulder notes that the first recorded rock climb in Colorado took place here in 1906 on the Third Flatiron. Today the surrounding open-space system contains more than fourteen hundred climbing opportunities.

blocks.title: Chautauqua beneath the Flatirons
blocks.text: At the base of the Flatirons is Chautauqua, where Boulder residents approved a bond issue in 1898 to purchase land for a Chautauqua assembly. More than a century later, the meadow and historic buildings remain one of the city's signature gateways into the mountains.

blocks.title: Longs Peak far to the left
blocks.text: As we continue north, Longs Peak is the major mountain target, but it is important to set the scale correctly: the summit is far to the left, roughly seventeen miles west of our viewing waypoint. This is a broad skyline view across the foothills, not a close mountain pass.

blocks.title: Finding Longs Peak
blocks.text: Look well left toward the high crest of Rocky Mountain National Park. Longs Peak rises to fourteen thousand two hundred fifty-nine feet and is the highest summit in the park. From this eastern side, its size and relatively isolated profile can make it stand out even from many miles away, weather permitting.

blocks.title: The Keyhole Route
blocks.text: Longs Peak is famous for the Keyhole Route, but the National Park Service emphasizes that it is a climb rather than a normal hike. The maintained trail ends at the Boulder Field, and the upper route requires scrambling across exposed ledges and steep rock where a fall can be fatal.

blocks.title: A mountain that makes its own schedule
blocks.text: Even in summer, Longs Peak can produce winter-like conditions and fast-changing weather. Afternoon thunderstorms are a major hazard, which is why climbers often begin in the dark and aim to be off the exposed upper mountain well before storms build.

blocks.title: Leaving the mountain view
blocks.text: We are turning away from the mountain wall now and heading toward Northern Colorado Regional Airport. Longs Peak will begin to slip behind and to the left as the plains open again ahead.

blocks.title: Loveland and Fort Collins corridor
blocks.text: The destination airport sits between Loveland and Fort Collins, two cities that have grown toward one another along the Front Range. Fort Collins developed around a military post and later Colorado State University, while Loveland grew with agriculture, rail connections and industries serving the northern Colorado region.

blocks.title: Back near Colorado State
blocks.text: Fort Collins is north of the airport, and Colorado State University remains one of the city's defining institutions. Founded in 1870 as the state's land-grant college, it grew from an agricultural school into a major research university while keeping strong ties to agriculture, veterinary medicine and the practical sciences.

blocks.title: Northern Colorado Regional Airport
blocks.text: Northern Colorado Regional Airport is just ahead. We have come full circle geographically on this leg: south from Cheyenne into Denver, west to the foothills, north along the mountain wall, and now back onto the plains between Loveland and Fort Collins.
